Applications/GHG-Fluxes.title: GHG Fluxes
Applications/GHG-Fluxes.content:
GHG Fluxes
Agricultural framing of how soil-applied biochar changes nitrous oxide (N₂O), methane (CH₄), and soil organic carbon priming / CO₂ fluxes. CDR credit math is still dominated by stable biochar carbon (Permanence, Biochar as Durable CDR); flux co-benefits are secondary and highly variable.
Sibling notes: Soil and Agriculture · Crop Yield Effects · Application Rates and Methods.
Summary table



































Gas / processTypical cited rangesCaveatsPrimary URLN₂OClassic meta ~−54% (Cayuela 2014); field-focused Jia 2023 −26.8%; Woolf inventory illustrative −23% year 1 onlyEffect fades / uncertain beyond year 1; H:C_org mattersdoi.org/10.1016/j.agee.2013.10.009 · doi.org/10.1002/ldr.4868 · doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.1c02425CH₄Jia 2023 global −13.0%; paddies sometimes stronger ↓; other metas often ns overallSystem-dependent (upland vs flooded)doi.org/10.1002/ldr.4868CO₂ / primingShort-term positive priming common; longer-term often negative priming (Wang 2016 mean SOC mineralization ~−4%; Weng 2017 decade-scale accrual)Do not apply Woolf 2021 N₂O inventory method to organic/forest soilsdoi.org/10.1111/gcbb.12266 · doi.org/10.1038/nclimate3276 · doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.1c02425GWP (Jia 2023)Combined GWP −7.7% in that global analysisBundled metric; read paper for boundariesdoi.org/10.1002/ldr.4868
N₂O — mechanisms and metas
Classic and follow-on metas
Cayuela et al. (2014) reviewed and meta-analyzed soil N₂O responses and reported a large mean reduction (~54% in that analysis) (DOI; author PDF mirror: digital.csic.es/bitstream/10261/273052/4/Cayuela2014AgricEcosysEnv.pdf).
Cayuela et al. (2015) show the molar H:C_org ratio is a key factor: more aromatic / lower H:C_org chars tend to mitigate N₂O more strongly (DOI). This is one scientific reason NRCS and EBC/IBI stress H:C_org < 0.7 (and producers chase lower still) — see NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag, Product Standards EBC IBI, Properties.
Mechanistic denitrification work (electron shuttling / buffering): Cayuela et al. (2013) Scientific Reports (DOI).
Field-oriented update
Jia et al. (2023) report global mean N₂O −26.8% under biochar application alongside yield and other GHG metrics (DOI). Treat this as more conservative than the 2014 laboratory-heavy mean.
Inventory / MRV conservatism (Woolf 2021)
Woolf et al. (2021) greenhouse-gas inventory method for biochar soil additions allows an optional N₂O adjustment of −23% for the first year only, and only when application exceeds 10 Mg C ha⁻¹; they assume no net CH₄ change for inventory simplicity (DOI). Organic and forest soils are out of scope for that optional credit.
Farm takeaway: do not budget large multi-year N₂O offsets into agronomic NPV unless measured on-site. Credit programs primarily remunerate durable C, not flux co-benefits (MRV Stack).
CH₄ — upland vs flooded systems

Jia et al. (2023): mean CH₄ −13.0% (DOI).
Rice paddies and other anaerobic systems can show reductions in some East Asian metas cited in secondary literature, but responses remain mixed (increases or non-significant results appear in the wider corpus). Site hydrology, labile C, and iron redox chemistry matter.
Woolf 2021 default: no net CH₄ change for national inventory–style accounting (DOI).

Priming and SOC stocks

























SourceFindingURLWang et al. 2016Decomposition + priming meta; mean SOC mineralization change ~−4% (negative priming on average)doi.org/10.1111/gcbb.12266Weng et al. 2017Field evidence of decade-scale negative priming / SOC accrualdoi.org/10.1038/nclimate3276Jia et al. 2023Broader GHG + productivity synthesis including soil C interactionsdoi.org/10.1002/ldr.4868
NRCS FAQ contrasts biochar’s multi-century C persistence framing (~60–80% remaining at 100 years in their cited range) with compost (~2–14%), while noting compost’s superior short-term nutrient/microbial pulse (FAQ PDF). Cross-check F_perm tables in Permanence / Quantitative Benchmarks (IPCC 2019 appendix).
Interactions with rate, blends, and management

Rate: Woolf’s optional N₂O inventory term only at >10 Mg C ha⁻¹ year 1 — far above many CPS 336 planning rates (~4 yd³/ac baseline) (Woolf; NRCS FAQ).
Compost / manure blends: can change labile C, moisture, and N availability that drive N₂O — see Biochar Compost and Manure Blends; Earth Foundries Napa trial reported process GHG co-benefit as VOC −33% during composting with 10% biochar (PDF) — a facility emission metric, not soil N₂O.
Fertilizer N: Ye et al. (2020) yield meta emphasizes fertilizer interactions (PDF); N rate also modulates N₂O baselines.

Real-world projects noting GHG / CDR co-benefits
These claim climate benefits primarily via soil C storage; flux claims should be read as supplementary:

Exomad Green — Puro CORC soil end-use + stated N₂O co-benefit language on facility page: puro.earth/cdr-credit-suppliers/facilities/exomad-green-concepcion/
Charm Range & Plains — Isometric soil land application: registry.isometric.com/project/prj_1JN6XNWDQ1S0BSN7
Oasis Vineyard — cites Woolf 2021 persistence (>80% projected 100-yr for high-T wood char used): pacificbiochar.com/wp-content/uploads/Oasis-Vineyard-Trial_-5th-harvest_-Final-Draft_12.12.2023.pdf

Applications/Real-World-Soil-Projects.content:
Real World Soil Projects
Named current or recent soil / agriculture deployments with outbound URLs. Only projects with verifiable primary or high-quality secondary sources are listed. Marketing claims without documentation are omitted. Companion: Soil and Agriculture · Crop Yield Effects · Biochar Compost and Manure Blends.
Report date: 2026-09-14.
Carbon-credit projects with verified soil end-use
Exomad Green — Concepción / Riberalta, Bolivia (Puro.earth)

Registry: Puro facility page states CORC 100+ durability; biochar from sawmill hardwood residues pyrolyzed ~600 °C; biochar donated to local Indigenous communities for agricultural soil enhancement (Puro — Exomad Green, Concepción).
Issuance (facility table on Puro page): 2023 21,252; 2024 58,344; 2025 102,458; 2026 91,457 CORCs (as published on page at fetch time).
Ag guidance: mix with inoculant; site-specific rates; planting-row / volume-% examples (Exomad biochar).
Field study (trade press, 2025-07-04): Santa Cruz trials — corn +15% (up to +32% with fertilizer + microbes); beans +13% (up to +25%) (Bioenergy International).
MRV partner case study: Carbonfuture — Exomad.

Verification note: Soil end-use is explicit on Puro and company pages (donation / farm application)—not a non-soil-only sink.
Charm Range & Plains Biochar — USA (Isometric)

Registry project: Charm co-produces bio-oil and biochar (Fort Lupton, CO) from wildfire-mitigation woody biomass; “We transport biochar via truck to various sites where it is sequestered via land application” (Isometric project).
Crediting period 01 Mar 2024 – 01 Mar 2029; issued volume shown on registry page; storage-site locations reported as secured upon offtake execution.
Company narrative: partners with farmers for water-stressed soils / productivity co-benefits; first Isometric CCP-labeled biochar credits (Charm blog).
Soil storage module reference: registry.isometric.com/module/biochar-storage-soil-environments/1.3

Verra Project 4679 — “Reignite,” Odisha, India (VM0044)

First project registered under VM0044 (announced 8 Oct 2024).
Rural farmers convert agricultural waste (instead of open burning) to biochar used on the same farms as a soil amendment (Verra news).
Methodology page: verra.org/methodologies/vm0044-biochar-utilization-in-soil-and-non-soil-applications-v1-2/

Commercial farms / vineyards (US)
Oasis Vineyard Trial — Monterey County, California

Partners: Sonoma Ecology Center, UC Riverside, Monterey Pacific Inc., Pacific Biochar; funded via California Department of Water Resources.
Pre-plant (2016–2017): biochar 10 t/ac, compost 15 t/ac, combo, vs control on sandy low-OM soils; incorporation ~30” in vine row.
Five harvests: combo +36%, biochar +25%, compost +29% average yield vs control; positive ROI by second harvest; incremental revenue by fifth harvest **9,752 / 12,569 / 14,937** per acre (biochar / compost / combo) at ~1,500/ton grapes; amendment costs (2016 delivered) biochar 240/ton**, compost **40/ton wet.
Primary source PDF: pacificbiochar.com/wp-content/uploads/Oasis-Vineyard-Trial_-5th-harvest_-Final-Draft_12.12.2023.pdf

Dominus Estate — Napa Valley, California

Pacific Biochar case study: 25 t/ac biochar cultivated to 36” on a 6-acre vineyard redevelopment after fallow; SOM-equivalent design discussion; earthworks fall/winter 2022, profile pit summer 2023.
URL: pacificbiochar.com/case-study-biochar-application-with-dominus-estate-in-napa-valley-after-2-years-fallow/

Sonoma Ecology Center × Napa Recycling — American Canyon pyrolysis (startup 2025)

23 Mar 2025 startup of CAL FIRE / Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund–supported facility converting surplus urban woodchips (A Plus Tree feedstock) to biochar at Napa Recycling; plan to blend with Napa Recycling compost for farm/garden customers (Sonoma Biochar Initiative, 17 May 2025).
Related SEC biochar program pages: sonomaecologycenter.org/biochar/

Earth Foundries × Napa Recycling — composting with biochar

2023 project report: 10% biochar addition to green/food-waste composting reduced VOCs 33%, accelerated curing, affected finished compost nutrient/salinity metrics (PDF).

Wakefield BioChar — NRCS CPS 336 channel & paper-mill partnership

Company overview of NRCS Soil Amendment 336 applications and discounted pricing for qualifying producers: wakefieldbiochar.com/learning-center/nrcs-program-and-biochar-overview/
DS Smith Riceboro, GA paper-mill ash → Wakefield soil products; company cites ~2 tons/acre average farm spreading: wakefieldbiochar.com/learning-center/ds-smith-partners-with-wakefield-to-convert-paper-mill-waste-to-useful-biochar/

US programs / demos (practice standard)

NRCS CPS 336 national standard & FAQ (rates, scenarios, biosolids exclusion): www.nrcs.usda.gov/resources/guides-and-instructions/soil-carbon-amendment-ac-336-conservation-practice-standard · nrcs-prod.azureedge.us/sites/default/files/2026-04/soil-carbon-amendment-ac-336-faq.pdf
Producer funding explainer (American Farmland Trust / Farmland Info hosting USBI-style guide): farmlandinfo.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2023/12/biochar_funding_for_US_producers_quick_guide_.pdf
USBI: biochar-us.org/
Note: publicly cited acreage totals for national EQIP 336 adoption are sparse in primary USDA statistical releases as of this research pass—treat state office reports as the authority when citing acres.

International field deployments (documented)






























LocationWhatURLNepalUrine-enhanced / liquid-enriched biochar fertilizers; pumpkin trial + 21 multi-crop trialsdoi.org/10.3390/agriculture5030723 · doi.org/10.1002/ldr.2761Brazil (Seropédica)Biochar on degraded pastures; environmental + CBAdoi.org/10.1038/s41598-019-47647-xBolivia (Exomad)Industrial production + farm soil use + yield trialslinks aboveIndia (Odisha, Verra 4679)Farm-waste biochar returned to farmsverra.org/verra-registers-first-biochar-project/
Australian mine-spoil and pasture trials exist in the peer-reviewed literature (e.g., acacia–biochar mine rehab DOI); treat as research deployments unless a named commercial operator page is added later.
How to read these cases

Credit project ≠ agronomic trial. Exomad/Charm/Verra prove soil sink pathways under MRV; yield numbers need separate trial reports.
Vineyard California cases are among the best public multi-year agronomic + economic datasets (Oasis PDF).
Composting co-benefits (VOC, curing) are facility metrics—do not equate to field N₂O (GHG Fluxes).
Always check feedstock (forest residue, urban wood, ag waste) against local residue-retention rules (NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag).

Applications/Soil-and-Agriculture.title: Soil and Agriculture
Applications/Soil-and-Agriculture.content:
Soil and Agriculture
Chapter-length map of biochar in farm and soil systems: how it changes soil, what yield and GHG metas say, how to apply it, named real-world deployments, products/practices, constraints, and links to Permanence, NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag, and carbon-market soil pathways.
Report context: 2026-09-14.
Purpose and scope
Most historical agronomy and a large share of voluntary biochar CDR still assume soil end-use. Outcomes are context-specific (texture, pH, climate, rate, feedstock/process, fertilizer regime). This note synthesizes primary metas, NRCS practice guidance, and named projects—not universal prescriptions.
Child / related notes

























































TopicNoteYield metas & field evidenceCrop Yield EffectsN₂O / CH₄ / priming (ag framing)GHG FluxesRates, incorporation, banding, NRCS scenariosApplication Rates and MethodsNamed farms, vineyards, credit projectsReal World Soil ProjectsCompost / manure co-applicationBiochar Compost and Manure BlendsInoculation / charging / BBFsBiochar Inoculation for FertilizerNutrients & fertilizer chemistryBiochar Nutrients and Fertilizer ChemistryMicrobes & soil biologyBiochar Microbes and Soil BiologyCost / benefit (sourced only)Agronomic EconomicsUS EQIP/CSP practiceNRCS CPS 336 and US AgPersistence of applied CPermanence · Permanence Science for CreditsContaminants / specsContaminants and Quality · Properties · Product Standards EBC IBI
1. Soil mechanisms
1.1 Water retention and physical structure
Meta-analyses generally show larger hydrological benefits in coarse-textured soils:

Omondi et al. (2016) quantified mean effects including available water capacity (AWC) +15.1%, porosity +8.4%, bulk density −7.6%, and saturated hydraulic conductivity +25.2% across compiled studies (DOI).
Razzaghi et al. (2020) systematic review/meta-analysis asks whether biochar improves water retention and finds texture- and rate-dependent gains (DOI).
Wei et al. (2023) (939 observations) report field capacity / AWC responses by texture: coarse FC +23.8% / AWC +25.6%; medium +5.0% / +20.9%; fine +7.2% / +11.5% (DOI).
Blanco-Canqui (2017) reviews physical-property pathways (bulk density, porosity, aggregation, hydraulics) as functions of rate, feedstock, and soil (DOI).

Practice implication: sandy / low-OM soils are the clearest hydrological use-case; fine clays may show smaller AWC gains for the same rate.
1.2 Nutrients, CEC, and liming / pH
Jeffery et al. (2011) interpreted stronger productivity responses in acidic (+14%) and coarse/medium soils as consistent with liming and water-holding mechanisms, plus improved nutrient availability (DOI). Jeffery et al. (2017) found mean tropical yield benefits (~+25%) versus little mean benefit in temperate systems, again consistent with acid / low-fertility soil chemistry (DOI).
USDA NRCS CPS 336 guidance (April 2026 FAQ) states biochar is usually alkaline and most useful as a liming agent on acid soils; on soils already pH > 7, check liming equivalency and add cautiously. The FAQ walks liming-offset arithmetic (e.g., 1 ton biochar/acre at 9% CaCO₃ liming equivalency offsets ~9% of a 1 ton lime recommendation) (NRCS FAQ PDF).
NRCS also flags electrical conductivity (EC) / salts: high-ash manure chars can raise salinity; wood chars are typically lower EC. Spec-sheet examples in the FAQ contrast high-C wood char (low EC) vs poultry-manure char (high EC, high P/K, high liming) (same FAQ).
CEC and nutrient sorption are feedstock- and aging-dependent; Lehmann et al. (2021) summarize nutrient and liming co-benefits in the broader CDR/agronomy framing (DOI). Fresh, uninoculated biochar can temporarily immobilize nutrients—NRCS explicitly warns that “fresh biochar … has a chance to reduce crop yields by binding and immobilizing nutrients” and recommends compost/manure charging (FAQ; national standard also: inoculate with compost, compost tea, or manure — CPS 336 2022 PDF).
1.2b Inoculation, charging, and biochar-based fertilizers
Fresh biochar can temporarily immobilize nutrients; NRCS and USBI therefore treat inoculation/charging as standard practice before agronomic use (NRCS FAQ; USBI Ag Guidelines; CPS 336 inoculate clause: 2022 PDF).
Three modes (full chapter Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer):

Nutrient charging — soak/impregnate with NPK solutions, urine, digestate, or manufacture BBFs (pre/post-pyrolysis). Melo et al. (2022) meta: BBFs +10% productivity vs fertilized controls (DOI). Scoping review of enrichment methods: Ndoung 2021.
Microbial inoculation — compost tea, PGP/AMF/EM on char carriers; meta shows gains vs biochar alone but weak commercial-field consistency (DOI). Habitat in raw field-aged char can be sparse (Quilliam 2013).
Co-composting (COMBI) — organic coating + nitrate capture; Kammann et al. (2015) untreated BC ~60% of control biomass vs co-composted up to ~305% (DOI); coating chemistry (Hagemann 2017); COMBI review (Antonangelo 2021).

Practice ranges (sourced): charge 1–3 weeks (USBI); co-compost roughly 5–15% biochar w/w early (Pacific white paper; Antonangelo); enriched fertilizers can work at ≪2 t ha⁻¹ root-zone (Schmidt 2017; urine protocol Schmidt 2015).
Credit/MRV: Puro soil amendment pure/mixed (AF1–AF2) remains eligible end-use; co-composting does not erase aromatic C stability for permanence chemistry (Hagemann 2017; Puro Biochar Methodology Edition 2025). Details: Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer §9.
1.2c Nutrients & fertilizer chemistry (chapter pointer)
Deep chemistry of N/P/K, CEC/AEC, liming, BBF formulations, and fertilizer-use efficiency: Biochar Nutrients and Fertilizer Chemistry. Headline metas: soil inorganic N mean ~−11% NH₄⁺ / −10% NO₃⁻ in the first year class of evidence (Nguyen 2017); BBFs at mean 0.9 t ha⁻¹ give +10% productivity vs fertilized controls (Melo 2022); biochar+fertilizer field synergy ~+15% (Ye 2020).
1.2d Microbes & soil biology (chapter pointer)
Habitat vs sparse colonization, inocula efficacy, AMF/PGPR, priming, and disease-suppression uncertainty: Biochar Microbes and Soil Biology. Key contrast: biota review (Lehmann 2011) vs sparse field colonization of wood char (Quilliam 2013); inocula meta favors local/fungal over commercial products (DOI).
1.3 Microbial habitat and SOC interactions
Porous carbon provides habitat and alters redox / sorption environments that shape N cycling (see GHG Fluxes). For native soil organic carbon:

Wang et al. (2016) meta-analysis reports mean negative priming of SOC mineralization on the order of ~−4% (with short-term positive priming common) (DOI).
Weng et al. (2017) document decade-scale negative priming and SOC accrual under biochar in a field context (DOI).

NRCS positions biochar as long-lived SOM support versus compost’s shorter labile pulse: FAQ cites research that roughly 60–80% of biochar C can remain after 100 years versus 2–14% for compost C, and that ~10 yd³ biochar can match 1-year soil-C increase of ~40 yd³ compost in their comparison framing (FAQ). Cross-check permanence math with Permanence and [Woolf et al. 2021].
2. Crop / agronomic evidence (summary)
Full tables live in Crop Yield Effects. Headline metas:








































SourceYield / productivity findingURLJeffery et al. 2011Grand mean ~+10% (subgroup means −28% to +39%)doi.org/10.1016/j.agee.2011.08.015Jeffery et al. 2017Tropical mean ~+25%; temperate mean little/no benefitdoi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aa67bdYe et al. 2020Biochar + fertilizer ~+15% vs fertilizer alone in field setwww.css.cornell.edu/faculty/lehmann/publ/SoilUseManage%2036%2C%202-18%202020%20Ye.pdfJia et al. 2023Overall crop yield +9.4%doi.org/10.1002/ldr.4868Schmidt et al. 2015 (Nepal pumpkin)Large gains from urine-enhanced low-dose biochardoi.org/10.3390/agriculture5030723Pandit/Schmidt et al. (21 Nepal trials)Biochar-based fertilizers across 13 cropsdoi.org/10.1002/ldr.2761
Decision rule of thumb (evidence-based, not a guarantee): expect stronger agronomic ROI where soils are acidic, coarse, low-OM, tropical/subtropical, or degraded; temperate fertile systems often need compost/manure blends, banding, or CDR/policy payments to pencil (see Agronomic Economics, [Jeffery 2017]).
3. GHG fluxes from agricultural soils
Deep dive: GHG Fluxes. For farm planning:

N₂O: Cayuela et al. (2014) classic meta ~−54% (DOI); field-focused Jia et al. (2023) ~−26.8% (DOI). H:C_org of the char is a key moderator (Cayuela 2015).
CH₄: Mixed; Jia 2023 global mean −13.0%; paddies and flooded systems need site-specific reading (DOI). Woolf et al. (2021) inventory method assumes no net CH₄ change for simplicity (DOI).
Inventory conservatism: Woolf 2021 optional N₂O credit only for applications >10 Mg C ha⁻¹ in year 1 (illustrative −23%), and not for organic/forest soils (DOI).

CDR credit tonnage is dominated by stable biochar C, not annual N₂O co-benefits—see Biochar as Durable CDR, MRV Stack.
4. Application methods (pointer)
Full practice note: Application Rates and Methods; blends: Biochar Compost and Manure Blends.

Research rates: often 5–50+ t ha⁻¹ (extremes to 100 t ha⁻¹ in Jeffery 2011) — not default farm advice (DOI).
Enriched fertilizers: agronomic doses can be <2 t ha⁻¹ when nutrient-loaded (Schmidt/Pandit line; DOI).
NRCS CPS 336 planning: FAQ — 4–10 cubic yards per acre is a good starting range; FY2024 100% biochar payment scenario assumes 4 yd³/ac; blend scenarios specify compost + biochar quantities (FAQ).
Incorporation: tillage, trenching, no-till drill/prills, manure injectors, fertigation of fines, permanent-bed mixing; surface-only on slopes risks wind/water loss (FAQ).
Pasture: CPS 336 allowed on pasture; not on native rangeland except facilitating Range Planting (550) or Critical Area Planting (342) (FAQ).

5. Real-world current applications (critical)
Named, sourced deployments are catalogued in Real World Soil Projects. Snapshot:







































































ProjectWhereWhatPrimary URLExomad Green (Puro CORC 100+)BoliviaIndustrial hardwood-residue biochar; soil donation to Indigenous/local farmers; Santa Cruz field trials (corn/bean yield gains reported 2025)Puro facility · Exomad biochar page · Bioenergy International 2025-07-04Charm Range & Plains (Isometric)USA (Fort Lupton CO production; farm land application)Wildfire-mitigation woody biomass → biochar sequestered via agricultural land applicationIsometric project · Charm blogOasis Vineyard trialMonterey County, CAPre-plant 10 t/ac biochar ± 15 t/ac compost; 5 harvests; combo +36% yield vs controlPDF reportDominus EstateNapa Valley, CA25 t/ac biochar cultivated to 36” on 6-acre redevelopmentPacific Biochar case studySEC / Napa Recycling American CanyonAmerican Canyon, CAUrban woodchips → biochar; blend with Napa Recycling compost (startup Mar 2025)Sonoma Biochar InitiativeEarth Foundries × Napa RecyclingNapa, CA10% biochar in green/food compost; VOC −33%, faster curing2023 project PDFVerra Project 4679 ReigniteOdisha, IndiaFirst VM0044 registration; farm-waste biochar returned to same farms as soil amendmentVerra 2024-10-08Wakefield + NRCS pathwayUSASupplier guidance for CPS 336 applicants; DS Smith paper-mill ash partnership for soil productsNRCS overview · DS SmithBrazil degraded pasturesSeropédica, RJField amendment + environmental/cost-benefit analysisDOINepal enriched fertilizersNepalLow-dose urine/liquid-enriched biochar fertilizers (multi-crop trials)DOI · DOI
Credit stacking warning: NRCS EQIP/CSP payments for CPS 336 are not carbon credits. Coexistence with voluntary CDR requires contractual double-claim prevention — Double Counting and Credit Ownership, NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag.
6. Products and practice

Standards: Product Standards EBC IBI — EBC, IBI, NRCS Table 3 (H:C_org <0.7, C_org >10%) (CPS 336 PDF).
Enriched / biochar-based fertilizers: Schmidt/Pandit Nepal results show low-dose, nutrient-loaded chars can outperform bulk raw char (DOI).
Named commercial lines (sourced marketing pages, not endorsements): Wakefield Original / CarbonBoost / Pro Garden Mix (page); Pacific Biochar compost–biochar bulk blends (page); Napa Recycling compost + SEC biochar blend pathway (SBI).
US directories / tools: USBI, NRCS Soil Carbon Amendment tools / Biochar Atlas references on NRCS soil-carbon-amendments page.

7. Constraints — when it does not help (or hurts)























































RiskEvidence / guidanceURLTemperate fertile soils, weak mean yieldJeffery 2017doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aa67bdFresh uncharged char → N immobilizationNRCS FAQnrcs-prod.azureedge.us/sites/default/files/2026-04/soil-carbon-amendment-ac-336-faq.pdfHigh-EC manure chars → salinityNRCS FAQsameAlkaline soils + high-liming charNRCS FAQsameBiosolids chars / PFASExcluded under CPS 336same FAQContaminated feedstocks (PAHs, metals)Contaminants and Quality; Jeffery 2011 biosolids subgroup −28% yielddoi.org/10.1016/j.agee.2011.08.015Over-application cost without yieldGalinato et al. 2011 economics; Oasis costsdoi.org/10.1016/j.enpol.2011.07.035 · Oasis PDFSurface application on erodible slopesNRCS: do not apply where runoff/wind loss significantFAQResidue stripping for feedstockCPS 336: residues needed for soil cover / forest health not eligible feedstock pathFAQ
8. How soil use connects to permanence and credits

Produce & test to low H:C_org → Properties, Permanence.
Apply to eligible sink (soil / compost / etc.) with chain-of-custody → MRV Stack.
Choose methodology (soil modules differ): Verra VM0044, Puro Biochar Methodology Edition 2025, Isometric Biochar Protocol (soil storage module: registry.isometric.com/module/biochar-storage-soil-environments/1.3), CSI Global Biochar C-Sink.
Separate agronomic value (water, nutrients, yield) from credit value (durable C) in farm budgets → Agronomic Economics, Market Volumes and Pricing.

9. Decision tree (evidence-based)
Use this as a planning screen—not a substitute for soil tests or NRCS planners.

Soil screen — Prefer candidates with low OM, coarse texture, or acidic pH (Jeffery 2011/2017; NRCS FAQ). Skip or pilot carefully if alkaline, high-EC, or already high-P with manure-char products (Jeffery 2011; Jeffery 2017; FAQ).
Product screen — Spec sheet: C_org, H:C_org (<0.7 for CPS 336), ash, EC, liming equivalent, metals, PAHs as required by market/standard (Contaminants and Quality; CPS 336 PDF).
Rate screen — Start near NRCS 4–10 yd³/ac unless a vineyard redevelopment or research protocol justifies higher (Oasis 10 t/ac; Dominus 25 t/ac) (FAQ; Oasis; Dominus).
Blend screen — Default to compost/manure charge for agronomy; consider co-composting if a local facility pathway exists (Biochar Compost and Manure Blends).
Placement screen — Band/row for perennials and low doses; broadcast+incorporate for field crops; avoid unprotected surface on HEL slopes (FAQ).
Finance screen — Model yield-only, yield+EQIP, and yield+CDR cases separately (Agronomic Economics; Galinato 2011).
MRV screen — If selling removals: registry choice, application evidence, ownership, no double claim with CPS 336 (MRV Stack, Double Counting and Credit Ownership).

10. Feedstock × soil matching



































Feedstock tendencyTypical agronomic flagsSourcesHigh-T wood / forest residueHigh C_org, low ash/EC; good durable C; needs nutrient chargeOasis forest-residue char (PDF); Exomad hardwood (page); NRCS wood vs manure spec examples (FAQ)Poultry / manure charsHigher nutrients, liming, salts; Jeffery 2011 poultry-litter yield subgroup strong; watch P and ECdoi.org/10.1016/j.agee.2011.08.015 · FAQBiosolidsContaminant / PFAS policy risk; excluded from CPS 336 cost-shareFAQUrban wood (arborist chips)Local circular pathway; test for contaminants; CA American Canyon examplesonomabiocharinitiative.org/sec-and-napa-recycling-pyrolysis-startup/Ag waste (open-burn alternative)Verra 4679 Odisha model — char returned to same farmsverra.org/verra-registers-first-biochar-project/
Residue ethics: CPS 336 disallows paying for char made from residues that should stay for soil cover or forest health (FAQ). Production side: Feedstocks, Production Hub.
11. Monitoring for dual agronomy + credit use
Minimum practical stack (operator checklist also in NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag):

Batch IDs, weigh tickets, moisture, lab H:C_org / C_org
Geotagged application polygons and rates (yd³/ac or t/ha)
Incorporation depth / method notes
Baseline and follow-up soil tests (pH, OM, P, EC, bulk density if hydrology is a claim)
Yield records by treatment strip where claiming agronomic ROI
5+ year record retention common in credit MRV expectations (MRV Stack)
Contract language: who owns CORCs/VCUs vs NRCS payment beneficiary

Isometric soil storage module (example of soil-environment requirements): registry.isometric.com/module/biochar-storage-soil-environments/1.3
Puro biochar methodology edition cluster: Puro Biochar Methodology Edition 2025
Verra VM0044 (soil and non-soil): verra.org/methodologies/vm0044-biochar-utilization-in-soil-and-non-soil-applications-v1-2/
12. Open research gaps (do not invent answers)

National EQIP/CSP acreage statistics for CPS 336 by year/state (need USDA program reports)
Long-term (>10 yr) temperate row-crop yield meta limited to modern enriched products
Standardized farmgate price indexes for bulk agricultural biochar (distinct from CORC prices)
Head-to-head N₂O field campaigns at CPS 336–realistic rates (≪ Woolf’s 10 Mg C ha⁻¹ inventory threshold)

13. Deep dive — water, CEC, and liming numbers
Hydrology metas (copyable figures)





















































MetricMean effectConditionsDOI / URLAWC+15.1%Omondi et al. 2016 global meta meandoi.org/10.1016/j.geoderma.2016.03.029Porosity+8.4%samesameBulk density−7.6%samesameKsat+25.2%samesameFC / AWC coarse soils+23.8% / +25.6%Wei et al. 2023doi.org/10.1016/j.geoderma.2023.116591FC / AWC medium+5.0% / +20.9%Wei 2023sameFC / AWC fine+7.2% / +11.5%Wei 2023same
Systematic review companion: Razzaghi et al. 2020 (DOI). Narrative physical-property review: Blanco-Canqui 2017 (DOI).
Liming arithmetic (NRCS worked example)
If soil test calls for 1 ton lime/ac and producer applies 1 ton biochar/ac with liming equivalency 9% CaCO₃, remaining lime need ≈ 0.91 ton/ac (FAQ). Using biochar only as a lime substitute does not meet CPS 336’s stated purposes if that is the sole intent—the FAQ warns against treating liming-as-purpose as 336-eligible framing.
CEC / nutrient sponge
Biochar’s surface functional groups and porosity can increase effective nutrient retention, but fresh high-temperature wood chars may have relatively low CEC until oxidized/aged or compost-charged. Operational guidance therefore emphasizes inoculation (CPS 336 PDF). Lehmann et al. 2021 synthesize nutrient and liming co-benefits in the CDR context (DOI).
14. Glossary (soil/ag)

AWC — available water capacity (plant-available water between field capacity and permanent wilting point).
Charging / inoculation — loading biochar with nutrients and/or microbes (compost, manure, teas, fertilizers) before or during application.
CPS 336 — NRCS Conservation Practice Standard Soil Carbon Amendment.
H:C_org — molar hydrogen to organic carbon ratio; lower ⇒ more aromatic / persistent; NRCS max 0.7.
Liming equivalency — % CaCO₃ neutralizing value of the amendment.
Priming — change in mineralization rate of native SOC after amendment (positive = faster loss; negative = slower).
yd³/ac — cubic yards per acre (NRCS contracting unit); convert with measured bulk density.

Carbon-Markets/Biochar-as-Durable-CDR.title: Biochar as Durable CDR
Carbon-Markets/Biochar-as-Durable-CDR.content:
Biochar as Durable CDR
Core pathway

Photosynthetic capture — Biomass stores atmospheric CO₂ (~45–50% C dry matter, depending on feedstock).
Thermochemical conversion — Pyrolysis or gasification (typically >350 °C, limited/no O₂) converts a substantial fraction into an aromatic carbon matrix (biochar); gases/oils must be accounted for in LCA.
Durable storage — Soil application, burial, or materials (concrete, asphalt, composites) so that a large fraction of organic C does not return to the atmosphere on multi-decadal to millennial timescales.

This is carbon dioxide removal (CDR) / biochar carbon removal (BCR) when the credited outcome is net atmospheric CO₂ stored in a durable reservoir, after subtracting lifecycle emissions and counterfactual storage.
CDR vs avoidance
Avoidance / reduction claims (displacing fossil fuels with pyrolysis heat; avoiding methane from waste) are a different claim. Most modern biochar removal methodologies deliberately credit durable storage of biochar carbon, not fossil displacement. Mixing removal and avoidance without clear boundaries is a common greenwashing critique—see Risks and Controversies.
Why treated as durable

Higher pyrolysis severity → lower H/C_org (and often O/C_org) → slower mineralization.
IPCC 2019 F_perm ≈ 0.65 / 0.80 / 0.89 by temperature class at ~20 °C baseline.
Woolf et al. (2021) refined with H/C_org + soil temperature. DOI: 10.1021/acs.est.1c02425
Petrographic approaches (Ro / inertinite) argue millennial persistence for highly condensed fractions (Sanei et al. 2024; DOI: 10.1016/j.coal.2023.104409).

Important: Standards do not typically credit 100% of biochar C—they apply permanence factors, LCA deductions, leakage, and (in some programs) mandatory offsetting of process emissions.
Soil / materials pathways
Dominant voluntary-market pathway for ag operators: soil application (direct spreading, compost/manure/digestate blends, or bedding/feed routes where allowed). Non-soil pathways (concrete, asphalt) also generate credits under Verra, Puro, Isometric, and CSI with different end-use evidence.

Carbon-Markets/Double-Counting-and-Credi.content:
Double Counting and Credit Ownership
Problem patterns

Same tonne, multiple claims — product “carbon footprint reduction,” voluntary credit, and compliance instrument simultaneously.
Value-chain ambiguity — grower, pyrolyzer, farmer, and credit buyer without clear ownership contracts. Isometric and CSI emphasize single credit owner + registry tracking.
Methodology overlap — soil-carbon farming methodologies and biochar CDR both claiming the same C.
Practice stacking — NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag cost-share payments coexist with voluntary CDR credits only if contracts prevent double claiming the same tonne.

Practical safeguards

Contractually assign who owns the climate claim before application
Retire unique registry tonnes; do not also market unretired “carbon-negative” product claims for the same mass
Disclose stacking of NRCS / other ag payments with credit issuance
Maintain chain-of-custody records (often ≥5 years)—see MRV Stack

MRV Stack
What is measured



































DomainTypical measurementsLab vs fieldFeedstockWaste/residue status, sustainability, counterfactual fate, transport, cultivation emissionsDocumentary + activity dataPyrolysisTemperature, residence time, O₂ exclusion, mass balance, energy use, flue-gas CH₄/N₂O/COContinuous sensors and/or periodic stack testsBiochar characterizationC_org, H/C_org, O/C_org, ash, moisture, metals, PAHs, PCDD/F, PCBs; optional Ro, HyPyAccredited lab (ISO 17025)Application / storageDry mass delivered & applied; GPS; incorporation; matrix mix ratios; custodyField / logistics evidencePermanenceModeled F_durable / GPC–SPC from lab properties ± soil TLab proxies + models
Why not field SOC stock change? Distinguishing biochar-C from native SOC at scale is difficult; standards credit characterized biochar applied to an eligible sink, discounted by permanence models—not measured ΔSOC.
Typical high-integrity characterization package

Proximate/ultimate: moisture, ash, VM, C/H/N/O/S
C_org (total C − inorganic C)
Molar H/C_org and O/C_org
Contaminants: Pb, Cd, Cu, Ni, Hg, Zn, Cr, As; PAHs; dioxins/furans; PCBs
Agronomic: pH, EC/salts, liming, nutrients
Advanced (program-dependent): Ro, BC_HyPy, Rock-Eval

Methods often cited: ASTM D5373 / D1762 / D4373; ISO 16948, 18134, 10390, 17025; ISO 7404-5 for Ro.
Common issuance pattern

Produce & characterize batch
Deduct LCA emissions (CSI: retire offsets from emission portfolio)
Prove eligible end use with custody trail
Apply permanence factor → issue credits ex post
Maintain records (often ≥5 years); monitor reversal risks

3. Why these buyers choose BCR
Synthesized from public statements collected in Snapshot 2025 (not invented):

Nasdaq additionally frames purchases as supporting marketplace scale and UN SDG co-benefits (Snapshot).

Why tiers matter commercially
CDR.fyi and corporate statements repeatedly cite integrity, durability, scalability, and co-benefits as purchase screens (e.g., Swiss Re, SEB, Nasdaq narratives in the Biochar Snapshot 2025). Price discovery is incomplete (few disclosed $/t on megadeals), so quality signalling often substitutes for transparent indexes outside Puro CORCs (Price Indexes and Benchmarks).

Whether CCP labels raise bilateral prices is not publicly quantified in CDR.fyi abridged posts—treat as a segmentation hypothesis, not a measured premium.
Permanence science vs commercial tiers
Commercial durability claims map to science stacks:

100-year inventory style: IPCC appendix; Verra VM0044 Table 3 (H/C_org) — CDR Potential and IPCC Accounting · Verra VM0044
Several centuries / CORC200+: Puro Edition 2025 power-law — Puro CORC200+ · Puro Biochar Methodology Edition 2025
200y or 1000y (Ro path): Isometric modules — Isometric Biochar Protocol
GPC >1000y vs SPC: CSI — CSI Global Biochar C-Sink

Debates: Consensus vs Debates · Permanence · Permanence Science for Credits.
Delivery quality (often under-weighted)
Buyers increasingly price near-term deliverability alongside permanence (Supercritical/Exomad Apr 2026 narrative; CDR.fyi “promise to proof”). A Tier-A method with weak operational delivery underperforms a Tier-A method with proven tonnes—see delivery ratios in Market Volumes and Pricing and supplier track records in Supply Landscape.
Gaps

No public, standardized BCR “grade” across registries.
Limited disclosed price differentials by tier.
dMRV platforms (e.g., Carbonfuture) appear in megadeal contracts but are not themselves a registry grade.

Market Volumes and Pricing
Chapter-length synthesis of biochar carbon removal (BCR) market volumes and price signals as of 2026-09-14. Figures are from primary / high-signal public sources only—chiefly CDR.fyi abridged reports and Puro × Nasdaq indexes. Do not treat this note as live market data; re-pull sources before diligence.
Related: Market Hub · Buyers and Offtakes · Historical Deals · Price Indexes and Benchmarks · Supply Landscape · Durable CDR Quality Tiers · Puro Pricing and CORC Indexes · Risks and Controversies

1. How to read the three volume metrics

























MetricWhat it measuresWhy it mattersContracted / purchasedForward offtakes + spot sales reported to trackersDemand & bankability; dominated by multi-year megadealsDeliveredTonnes actually issued / delivered ex-postOperational proof; BCR leads all durable CDR methods hereRetiredTonnes cancelled on a registry for a climate claimFinal use of the credit; liquidity + claim integrity
CDR.fyi tracks durable removals (hundreds to thousands of years permanence). Coverage claim in Q1 2026 notes: ~97%+ of publicly disclosed durable CDR contract volume (methodology caveats).

2. Cumulative BCR volumes (Q1 2022 → H1 2025)
Primary source: Biochar Carbon Removal Market Snapshot 2025 (published 2025-09-09).
Headline table

Growth narrative

2022–2024: purchase tonnage roughly tripled year-over-year; 2024 purchases exceeded all prior years combined.
Q2 2025: largest BCR quarter ever, driven by Microsoft–Exomad Green ≥1.24 Mt (Exomad May 2025; Historical Deals).
Deliveries and retirements roughly doubled annually 2022–2024; Q1–Q2 2025 retirements were closer to flat vs year-ago quarters (+12% / +0.4%).

5. Price trends — index vs bilateral
5.1 Public index (Puro × Nasdaq)
Retrieved 2026-09-14 from Puro Carbon Removal Indexes:

CORCCHAR < CORCX in this snapshot: biochar trades at a discount to the all-CORC composite on reported near-term Puro transactions—not proof of a global BCR discount vs Verra/Isometric/CSI.
5.2 Survey / disclosed-order pricing (CDR.fyi)






























ObservationDetailCaveatAll-method WAP ↓490 → 320 / t (2023→2024) (YIR)Mix of DAC, BECCS, EW, BCR, etc.Biochar ↑+18% YoY (YIR)Exact BCR mean undisclosed in abridged YIRNarrow BCR bandYIR says biochar settled into a “relatively narrow price range”No numeric band published in abridged postMegadeal unit pricesGenerally not in press releasesMajor transparency gap
5.3 Index vs bilateral offtakes

























ChannelCharacteristicsIndex (CORCCHAR)Near-term reported CORC trades; transparent €/t level; Puro-onlySpot platform inventoryCertified tonnes; may track near indexMulti-year offtakesFirm + optional volumes; prices usually confidential; may embed delivery risk, co-benefits, dMRV requirementsIntermediated portfoliosSupercritical, Senken, Watershed, Patch, Carbonfuture, etc.; 74% of Q1 2026 tonnes
Science-side abatement cost ranges (e.g., literature ~$70–360/t) are not credit market prices—see Quantitative Benchmarks.
5.4 Quality-tier effects on price
Public abridged sources do not quantify CCP-label or 1000-year-path premiums in $/t. Practical segmentation hypotheses (unverified price deltas):

Buyers requiring CCP methodology labels today may prefer Verra VM0044 VCUs.
Buyers requiring 1000-year Ro / burial may prefer Isometric Biochar Protocol (e.g., Carba–Microsoft).
Buyers optimizing near-term delivery + CORCCHAR discovery may prefer Puro CORC200+ inventory.
Uncertified marketing claims should clear at zero credit value for neutralization accounting (Durable CDR Quality Tiers).


6. Liquidity & cycle time

























SignalFigureSourcePuro biochar CORC issuance → transfer/retirement95 days (2021) → 22 days (mid-2025)Snapshot 2025 citing Puro Aug 2025 reportRetired : delivered (BCR cumulative)~50% by end-Q2 2025Snapshot 2025Intermediary share of Q1 2026 tonnes74%Q1 2026
Faster CORC turnover improves working-capital dynamics for suppliers on the Puro stack (Puro Project Cycle and MRV · Puro Pricing and CORC Indexes).

7. Why buyers choose BCR (volume implications)
From Snapshot business-case synthesis (Swiss Re, SEB, Tide, Nasdaq, and diversified majors):

Rapid contracting → delivery relative to DAC/BECCS.
Lower prices relative to many engineered methods (qualitative; exact differentials sparse).
Ability to start small (<100 t trials) — explains 290 unique purchasers.

These structural advantages explain why BCR can be ~10% of contracted durable CDR yet ~86–92% of delivered/retired tonnes.

2. CORCX and CORCCHAR — snapshot (as of retrieval)
Source: Puro Carbon Removal Indexes, retrieved 2026-09-14:

How to read them

Transaction-based: Indexes track reported near-term CORC transactions under a Nasdaq methodology—not a theoretical model price.
Puro-only: Levels apply to CORCs under the Puro Standard. They are not quotes for Verra Verra VM0044 VCUs, Isometric Biochar Protocol credits, or CSI Global Biochar C-Sink C-sinks.
Near-term bias: Designed for price discovery on inventory that trades soon—not a perfect proxy for 10-year offtake strike prices.
CORCCHAR vs CORCX: In Aug 2026, biochar sat ~€15 below the all-CORC composite. That gap can reflect pathway mix (other CORC methods in CORCX), liquidity, and timing—not a global “biochar discount” law.
EU benchmark caveats: Puro notes potential qualification as a benchmark under Regulation (EU) 2016/1011 for certain financial uses—read the factsheet before referencing in contracts.
More indexes planned as other methodologies gain transaction density (Puro page statement).

Full commercial context (fees, offtake waiver, liquidity days): Puro Pricing and CORC Indexes · Puro.earth Overview.

Carbon-Markets/Methodologies/CSI-Global-.title: CSI Global Biochar C-Sink
Carbon-Markets/Methodologies/CSI-Global-.content:
CSI Global Biochar C-Sink
Operator: Carbon Standards International AG (CSI), with Ithaka Institute (formerly “EBC Biochar C-Sink”)
Registry: Global C-Sink Registry
Current version: Global Biochar C-Sink Standard 3.3 (valid since 9 June 2026); v3.2 from 15 November 2025
PDF: 4000039EN.pdf
Prerequisite
Only EBC- or WBC-certified biochar may receive Global Biochar C-Sink certification. Product class must match use (e.g., EBC-Agro / WBC-Agro for agricultural soil).
What it credits
A tracked C-sink (not avoidance):

















PoolMeaningGPCGeologically persistent carbon (>1000 years; eligible for CO₂ offsetting under CSI logic)SPCSemi-persistent carbon (decays over ≤1000 years; temporary climate services / methane offsetting)
Persistence classes (v3.3)





















ConditionSplitH/C_org > 0.40100% SPC, 0% GPCH/C_org ≤ 0.40 (lower class)75% GPC / 25% SPCUpper class: mean Ro ≥ 3.8% or BC_HyPy ≥ 90%90% GPC / 10% SPC
Emission portfolio
All associated GHG from biomass → application must be registered and offset (fossil CO₂/N₂O with GPC; CH₄ with temporary sinks delivering TCE over 5–20 years) before C-sink validation.

Margin of safety 20 kg CO₂e / t biochar (DM)
Fossil process emissions must fall below 100 kg CO₂e / t biochar by 2030 and 20 kg by 2035
Process energy-use efficiency rule (>60% in exec summary); carbon-efficiency / additionality checks

Other

Global Artisan C-Sink — separate CSI standard for distributed/artisanal production
ICVCM: CSI submitted Global C-Sink Standards for assessment (materials dated 2026)—treat as in process, not automatic CCP approval

Carbon-Markets/Methodologies/Isometric-B.content:
Isometric Biochar Protocol
Operator: Isometric (registry + Certify platform)
Current version: Biochar Production and Storage v1.3

Protocol
Soil storage module

Modules also cover built environment & low-oxygen burial; production modules for combustion co-product, distributed/small-scale, and mobile reactors. ICVCM / ICROA / CORSIA accreditation claimed on protocol pages.
What it credits
Ex-post net CO₂e removal = stored − counterfactual − lifecycle emissions. Credits only after durable storage.
Soil MRV highlights

Batch-level (or statistically conservative Method B) measurement of C, moisture, H, inorganic C → C_org, H/C_org, O/C_org
Eligibility: H/C_org < 0.5, O/C_org < 0.2; heavy metals / PAH / PCDD/F / PCB limits meeting or exceeding WBC guidance
Labs: ISO 17025 (or agreed equivalent); ≥3 samples per measured batch preferred
End-use proof: geotagged application, GIS/logs, mixing evidence (biochar <50% v/v in matrices), affidavits/sales docs, chain of custody ≥5 years
Pyrolysis emissions: continuous monitoring or accredited periodic testing; CH₄/N₂O accounting

Permanence options (soil)

















OptionBasis200-yearConservative Woolf et al. (2021)–based decay using H/C_org + mean annual soil T (coefficients a=-0.383, b=0.350, c=-0.048; F_durable capped at 0.95; soil T floor 7 °C)1000-yearRandom reflectance with inertinite benchmark R₀ ≥ 2%, applied to non-reactive C fraction, credited at mean − 1 SD (Sanei et al. 2024 framework)
Additionality & buffer

Project-specific per Isometric Standard; reassessed if financials/regulations change; non-additionality stops future crediting only
Soil module typically 0% buffer under “No Observable Risk” framing (durability discounting built into quantification)

Parent concept: Puro CORC200+
Operator: Puro.earth Overview

This is the vault’s exhaustive note on Puro’s current biochar methodology: Edition 2022 → 2025 evolution, permanence modeling, eligibility, feedstock, end uses, LCA boundaries, and phase-out dates. Facts below are drawn from the Puro deep-dive research (2026-09-14) and primary PDFs/URLs cited there — not invented.
Primary PDF: Edition 2025 v2 — For Publication
Transition PDF: Methodology Transition Plan for Biochar Edition 2025 (2025-08-10)
Science cross-links while reading: Permanence · Permanence Science for Credits · Properties · Production · Contaminants and Quality · MRV Stack

Versions at a glance

Introduces CORC200+, revised power-law permanence model, stricter Biomass Sourcing Criteria, mobile facility rules, Table 3.2 overhaul. Who can list (supplier eligibility)

CO₂ Removal Supplier = biochar producer or contracted representative with sole CORC claim rights and end-to-end data access (rules 2.1.1–2.1.3)
Must comply with methodology + Puro Standard General Rules + local law
Path: Facility Audit (initial, typically on-site) → Certified Facility → Output Audits (at least annually) → CORC issuance

Operational detail: Puro Project Cycle and MRV

Feedstock rules (Biomass Sourcing Criteria)

Allowed categories potentially generating CORCs include:

Additional operational feedstock rules

Production requirements

Thermochemical conversion: pyrolysis / gasification / modified combustion / other
H/C_org < 0.70 mandatory (rule 3.5.1) — hard gate for quantification eligibility
Reactor categorization: mode, process, heating, streams, co-product fate
Combustion of volatiles: design for complete combustion; ≥95% normal combustion operating time; flameout procedures; CH₄/N₂O monitoring rules
Fossil fuel use allowed for ignition/support if no fossil C enters biochar and LCA includes emissions (coal as process fuel not allowed)

Facility baselines under Edition 2025:





















Baseline typeIntentNew FacilityGreenfield / new installationRetrofit FacilityConversion / upgrade of existing equipmentCharcoal RepurposePrior charcoal production redirected into eligible CDR pathway
Retrofit / charcoal-repurpose baselines deduct prior char storage via Eqs. 6.6–6.9 (see quantification section below).
Mobile rules (Edition 2025): explicit Stationary vs Mobile facility definitions; spatial extent within one host country; fleet rules. Common US pitfall when units cross state lines that imply multi-country or unclear host-country scope — see Puro Project Cycle and MRV.

Source: Dec 2025 retail update
Even with v2 safeguards, consumer channels remain higher-risk than contracted farm application (Risks and Controversies).

Additionality / baseline
Three components (rule 3.3.1):

Carbon additionality
Regulatory additionality
Financial additionality

Per Puro Additionality Assessment Requirements + Baseline and Additionality Questionnaire (made public after successful Facility Audit).
Biochar-specific financial analysis must cover:

Biochar sales prices
Co-product revenues
Cost structure

Pitfall: waste-treatment cost-saving projects may fail financial additionality if savings alone make the project viable without CORCs (rule 3.3.4). See Puro Project Cycle and MRV · Risks and Controversies.

Lifecycle emissions, leakage, and net CORCs
Overall equation (5.2.1):
[
\mathrm{CORCs} = C_{\mathrm{stored}} - C_{\mathrm{baseline}} - C_{\mathrm{loss}} - E_{\mathrm{project}} - E_{\mathrm{leakage}}
]





























TermMeaning(C_{\mathrm{stored}})Stored biochar C as CO₂e: (Q_{\mathrm{biochar}} \times C_{\mathrm{org}} \times 44/12) (Eq. 6.1)(C_{\mathrm{baseline}})Removals that would have occurred anyway (incl. retrofit / charcoal-repurpose deductions via Eqs. 6.6–6.9)(C_{\mathrm{loss}})Expected decay losses via persistence fraction PF (Eq. 6.3 conceptually: (C_{\mathrm{stored}} \times (100 - PF)/100) with PF in %)(E_{\mathrm{project}})Full LCA operational + embodied emissions; allocation to co-products; cut-offs(E_{\mathrm{leakage}})Identify, mitigate, quantify residual market/activity-shifting leakage
Net CDR logic in words: Stored biochar C (as CO₂e) minus expected decay losses minus baseline removals that would have occurred anyway minus project LCA emissions minus unmitigated leakage — only for biochar proven in an eligible end use.

Puro’s permanence stance vs millennial claims
Puro explicitly stopped at centuries, not millennia, pending integration of inertinite/Ro science (permanence post). Ro is encouraged for reporting but does not change CORC quantification under Edition 2025. Contrast with Isometric Biochar Protocol (200y or Ro≥2% → 1000y) and CSI Global Biochar C-Sink (upper GPC path via Ro≥3.8% or HyPy≥90%). Concept note: Puro CORC200+.

Reversal policy

No default buffer deduction (rule 4.2.1)
Risks managed via use eligibility + evidence
Supplier liable for reversals caused by non-compliance

Critics may prefer pooled buffers — see Risks and Controversies · Puro vs Other Standards.

Crediting period and renewals





















ItemEdition 2025Initial crediting period10 yearsRenewalsTwice, via new Facility Audit against latest rulesEdition 2022 hard stop12 Jun 2030
Capacity expansion of similar reactors may be possible without resetting period (rules 3.1.6–3.1.8 — detail in Puro Project Cycle and MRV).

ICVCM status for this methodology
As of ICVCM announcement 2025-12-11 and research date 2026-09-14:

Puro program is CCP-Eligible (General Rules v4.2+)
Biochar methodology is not yet CCP-Approved

Buyers wanting CCP-labelled credits today may prefer Verra VM0044 until Puro’s category assessment completes. Re-check ICVCM Assessment Status before relying on this. See Puro.earth Overview · Puro vs Other Standards.

When this methodology is the right fit
Prefer Edition 2025 / CORC200+ when you want:

Mature BCR buyer recognition + CORCCHAR price signal + Nasdaq registry infrastructure
Flexible baselines (New / Retrofit / Charcoal Repurpose) and explicit mobile fleet rules
A centuries-scale (200+) permanence claim with open-source PF model

Consider alternatives when you need CCP methodology labels today (Verra VM0044), a 1000-year Ro path (Isometric Biochar Protocol), or EBC/WBC-native GPC/SPC (CSI Global Biochar C-Sink). Full chooser: Puro vs Other Standards.

One-sentence definition
CORC200+ is Puro’s Edition 2025 biochar credit label asserting net durable CDR with a permanence framing of several centuries (≥200 years), quantified with a revised power-law decay model (H/C_org + soil temperature, 80% CI lower bound), and issued ex-post only after biochar reaches a durable eligible use.

Why the rename matters commercially

Buyers and offtake term sheets increasingly distinguish 100-year, 200-year / centuries, and 1000-year / millennial claims (Puro vs Other Standards · Buyers and Offtakes).
Marketing baseline CORCs still often say “100+ year durability” across pathways; biochar Edition 2025 specifically issues CORC200+ — do not conflate pathway-generic CORC marketing with the biochar label.
CCP methodology labels are a separate integrity layer: Puro program eligible ≠ biochar method CCP-Approved (Puro.earth Overview).


Permanence claim — what is asserted, what is not
Asserted

Quantification horizon of 200 years under a power-law persistence model.
After 200 years, deeper-soil protection is assumed for further centuries → marketing/label claim of several centuries / CORC200+.
Conservatism via the lower bound of an 80% confidence interval.
Soil temperature from Puro dataset with a 7 °C floor; H/C_org domain 0–0.7.

Not asserted (yet)

Millennial / 1000+ year inertinite-equivalent permanence as a quantified CORC factor.
That Ro (random reflectance) changes the number of CORCs — it is encouraged reporting only.
That program CCP-Eligibility equals a CCP credit label on biochar CORCs.

Puro explicitly stopped at centuries, not millennia, pending integration (permanence post). Contrast:

Common confusions (quick FAQ)
Is every CORC a CORC200+?
No. CORC200+ is the biochar Edition 2025 label. Other Puro methodologies use other durability labels (100+ / 200+ / 1,000+ depending on pathway).
Is CORC200+ the same as a 1000-year credit?
No. Puro stopped at centuries. Millennial claims live elsewhere (e.g., Isometric Ro path, CSI GPC upper class).
Does Ro unlock more CORCs under Puro?
Not yet. Encouraged reporting only; does not change quantification under Edition 2025.
Does CCP-Eligible program status put a CCP label on my biochar CORCs?
Not by itself. Methodology-category approval is separate; as of 2025-12-11 biochar was not yet CCP-Approved.
When is the credit created?
At first durable eligible use + successful Output Audit — not at the kiln door alone.

Generic MRV framing: MRV Stack
This chapter walks the full path from listing a facility to retiring CORCs: audits, lab metrics, chain of custody, auditor allocation, public fees, and a practical US producer path with common pitfalls. Facts from the Puro deep-dive research (2026-09-14) and primary fee/V&V documents cited there.

End-to-end cycle (one page)
Initial Qualification

        ↓

        ↓
Output Report → Output Audit (≥ annually)
        ↓
CORC issuance → transfer / sale → Buyer retirement

Critical rule: Point of CORC creation = first durable eligible use (rule 2.3.1) — ex-post relative to application, not factory gate alone. Claiming credits before use proof is a top failure mode. Practical path for a US biochar producer
Recommended sequence

Confirm feedstock fit against BSC categories (avoid A, J; understand P = processable but no CORCs).
Map end-use channel to Table 3.2 before promising buyers CORC volumes (farm contracts vs retail R3).
Submit Initial Qualification → Platform Agreement + KYC → MyPuro.
Register Production Facility (Stationary vs Mobile; host-country spatial extent for fleets).
Build Audit Package early: biomass evidence, LCA (stockpile CH₄, impurities, sludge fossil C, transport), Monitoring Plan, additionality questionnaire (especially financial additionality), permits, SDG/safeguards.
Optional Preliminary Assessment — remember 2022 PAs are obsolete for Edition 2025.
Facility Audit (VVB allocated by Puro).
Produce, apply, monitor → Output Audit → issuance → sell/retire.
Budget annual €1,400 + volume service tiers + retirement €0.25 (or offtake waiver).

Edition 2025 transition checklist

























SituationActionNew registration on/after 1 Nov 2025Must use Edition 2025Pre-launch registration, not yet auditedPrefer 2025; 2022 only if complete Audit Package by 15 Dec 2025Certified under 2022Finish current period; renew on latest edition; optional early upgrade at next Output AuditPlanning beyond 12 Jun 2030Edition 2022 terminated — design for 2025 now

Common pitfalls (from deep dive)

Weak waste/residue / BSC evidence; mixing ineligible feedstock (A, J) or issuing CORCs on category P
Claiming CORCs before eligible end-use proof
Retail / diffuse channels without R3 safeguards / RDF
Underestimating LCA — stockpile CH₄, plastic impurities, sludge fossil C, transport
Failing financial additionality when biochar product margins / waste-treatment savings already make the project viable without CORCs
Mobile fleet spatial-extent / multi-state host-country issues
Lab cadence shortfalls; H/C_org ≥ 0.70 batches
Edition 2022→2025 transition — renewals must meet 2025; Preliminary Assessments don’t transfer
Double counting across registries or intermediaries — Double Counting and Credit Ownership
Assuming CCP credit labels from program eligibility alone — biochar methodology not yet CCP-Approved (Puro.earth Overview · Puro vs Other Standards)

Broader market/integrity risks: Risks and Controversies

When to choose Puro vs other standards (ops lens)

















Choose Puro when…Choose Verra VM0044 when…Choose Isometric when…Choose CSI when…Mature BCR buyer recognition + CORCCHAR price signal + Nasdaq registry ops; mobile/retrofit/charcoal-repurpose fitNeed CCP-labelled methodology today + VCS buyer familiarity; clearly new waste facilityBuyer demands 1000-year Ro path or maximal soil MRV stringencyAlready hold EBC/WBC and want GPC/SPC + EU CRCF alignment path; artisan track
Many large buyers are registry-agnostic on BCR but diligence MRV; dual pathways are uncommon for the same tonne (double-counting rules). Full comparison: Puro vs Other Standards · peer notes: Verra VM0044 · Isometric Biochar Protocol · CSI Global Biochar C-Sink

Why comparison matters
Biochar carbon removal (BCR) buyers often diligence MRV stringency, permanence claim, and integrity labels more than brand alone. The same physical tonne generally cannot be credited under two registries (Double Counting and Credit Ownership). Choosing a pathway early locks feedstock rules, end-use evidence, and offtake narratives for years — especially under Puro’s Edition 2022 → 2025 transition through 2030.

Puro.earth Overview
Puro.earth is an engineered carbon dioxide removal (CDR) standard, registry, and market-infrastructure company based in Helsinki (Puro.earth Oy). It does not operate as a conventional multi-sector offset registry: CORCs are framed exclusively as durable removals, with avoidance kept out of CORC accounting.
This note is the map of the Puro cluster in the vault. Open child notes for depth; do not treat this overview as a substitute for the methodology or MRV chapters.
Why it matters for biochar
Biochar carbon removal (BCR) has been one of Puro’s longest-running pathways. Under Puro Biochar Methodology Edition 2025, biochar CORCs are labelled CORC200+ (“several centuries,” ≥200 years), with public price discovery via Nasdaq × Puro  CORCX indexes. For a US producer choosing among registries, start here, then read Puro vs Other Standards and Puro Project Cycle and MRV.
Related vault concepts: Biochar as Durable CDR · Permanence Science for Credits · MRV Stack · Market Hub · Market Volumes and Pricing · Buyers and Offtakes · Historical Deals · Price Indexes and Benchmarks · Risks and Controversies

What a CORC is
A CO₂ Removal Certificate (CORC) = 1 metric tonne CO₂e net removal, independently verified under a Puro methodology, recorded in the Puro Registry, transferable, and retired when applied to a climate claim (CORC page).
General marketing still frames “100+ year durability” as the baseline CORC definition across pathways. Biochar Edition 2025 specifically issues CORC200+.

How Puro fits the CDR / BCR market

Removal-only product. CORCs are engineered-CDR certificates; they are not a general-purpose offset unit mixing avoidance and removal.
Ex-post issuance after use. For biochar, the point of CORC creation is the first durable eligible use, not the factory gate alone — see Puro Project Cycle and MRV.
Public price signal. Unlike most BCR pathways, Puro publishes Nasdaq-methodology indexes (CORCX, CORCCHAR) — see Puro Pricing and CORC Indexes · Market Volumes and Pricing.
Buyer recognition. Early Microsoft CORC procurements and CDR.fyi BCR Snapshot 2025 buyer lists (Microsoft, Google, BCG, JPMorgan, Swiss Re, SEB with explicit Puro/CORC narrative) place Puro among the most recognizable BCR venues — see Buyers and Offtakes.
Liquidity trend. CDR.fyi (citing Puro Aug 2025 report): biochar CORC issuance→transfer/retirement time improved from 95 days (2021) to 22 days (mid-2025).

Key MRV themes

Carbon-Markets/Risks-and-Controversies.title: Risks and Controversies
Carbon-Markets/Risks-and-Controversies.content:
Risks and Controversies
Permanence science divergence
Decomposition-model camp (IPCC, Woolf 2021, Puro CORC200+, Isometric 200y) vs inertinite/Ro camp (Sanei et al.; Isometric 1000y; CSI upper class). Critiques argue inertinite proxies can overstate absolute permanence or that two-pool models mis-specify chemistry. See Permanence Science for Credits and Consensus vs Debates.
Leakage & land-use

Market leakage if biomass is diverted from higher-carbon uses (timber, mulch, animal feed)
Harvesting that depletes ecosystem carbon stocks (non–waste biomass) undermines net removal
Residue removal can harm soil protection (also flagged in NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag)

Contamination & agronomic harm
PAHs, dioxins, heavy metals, high salts (manure chars), excessive liming on alkaline soils; dust/albedo/erosion on slopes. Standards respond with EBC/WBC limits; NRCS excludes biosolids chars over PFAS concerns. See Contaminants and Quality.
Double counting
Same tonne claimed as product footprint reduction, voluntary credit, and compliance instrument; unclear ownership along grower → pyrolyzer → farmer → buyer chain; overlap with soil-carbon farming methodologies. See Double Counting and Credit Ownership.
Overstated yields / MRV gaps
Crediting before application; weak retail chain-of-custody; optimistic permanence factors; ignoring CH₄ from pyrolysis or biomass storage. Delivery vs contracted volume gaps create expectation risk ([CDR.fyi](www.cdr.fyi/blog/biochar-carbon-removal-market-snapshot-2025)).
Greenwashing critiques
NGOs (e.g., Fern, Carbon Market Watch) criticize carbon-removal certification frameworks—including biochar under EU CRCF drafts—for weak life-cycle boundaries, land-sector interactions, or insufficient safeguards. Marketing “carbon-negative fertilizer” without retired, unique registry tonnes is a separate risk.
Buyer concentration
Microsoft and a few others dominate BCR volume—see Buyers and Offtakes · Market Volumes and Pricing · Historical Deals. Q1 2026 intermediaries facilitated 74% of contracted tonnes (CDR.fyi).

Policy-and-Programs/NRCS-CPS-336-and-US-.content:
NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag
USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service Conservation Practice Standard 336 — Soil Carbon Amendment: EQIP/CSP (and related) cost-share for applying biochar and/or compost to improve soil health and store carbon. This is a conservation practice standard, not a carbon-credit methodology. Pair with Soil and Agriculture, Application Rates and Methods, Biochar Compost and Manure Blends, Double Counting and Credit Ownership.
Official documents (outbound)

































DocumentURLNational CPS 336 page (downloads + state links)www.nrcs.usda.gov/resources/guides-and-instructions/soil-carbon-amendment-ac-336-conservation-practice-standardNational standard PDF (Nov 2022)www.nrcs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2022-11/336-NHCP-CPS-Soil-Carbon-Amendment-2022.pdfPlanning FAQ (April 2026)nrcs-prod.azureedge.us/sites/default/files/2026-04/soil-carbon-amendment-ac-336-faq.pdfSoil Carbon Amendments overview / toolswww.nrcs.usda.gov/conservation-basics/natural-resource-concerns/soil/soil-health/soil-carbon-amendmentsProducer funding quick guide (Farmland Info hosting)farmlandinfo.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2023/12/biochar_funding_for_US_producers_quick_guide_.pdfABI / biochar.org funding guidelines PDF (2026)biochar.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Biochar-Guidelines-Funding-2026-final.pdf
What CPS 336 is for
Stated purposes include improve/maintain SOM, sequester/enhance soil C stocks, improve aggregate stability, and improve habitat for soil organisms; producers may also seek moisture and productivity co-benefits (FAQ). Sandy, acidic, less-healthy soils are called out as more likely to respond.
Biochar eligibility specs (practice)
From national standard Table 3 / narrative (2022 PDF):

Produced >350 °C under limited oxygen (pyrolysis or gasification)
Organic carbon (C_org) > 10% dry weight
H:C_org < 0.7 (molar) — lower preferred for sequestration
Metals and pathogens within Table limits; report ash, liming equivalent, nutrients, etc.
IBI Certified seal or documented Table 3 methods — but FAQ: certificate alone is not enough; planner still needs the spec sheet (FAQ)

Explicit exclusions / restrictions

No biosolids / municipal waste biochar or compost under 336 (PFAS and related concerns) (FAQ)
Residues that should remain for soil cover or forest health cannot be diverted into paid 336 feedstock pathways (FAQ)
Humic/fulvic products are not stand-alone carbon amendments under 336 (may be inoculants) (FAQ)

Planning rates and FY2024 scenarios
FAQ: 4–10 cubic yards per acre is a general starting range; characteristics of soil and amendment drive the final rate (FAQ).








































FY2024 scenario (FAQ Table 1)CompostBiochar100% Biochar (acres unit)—4 yd³/ac20% biochar / 80% compost4.4 t/ac0.8 yd³/ac40% biochar / 60% compost3.3 t/ac1.6 yd³/ac60% biochar / 40% compost2.2 t/ac2.4 yd³/ac80% biochar / 20% compost1.1 t/ac3.2 yd³/acCompost off-site3 t/ac—
Cubic-yard and small-area (ft²) scenarios exist for non-standard rates. Dry weight of 1 yd³ biochar ≈ 135–540 lb (FAQ).
Payment construction example: FY2023 60/40 blend scenario ~$160/yd³ average-cost build (state-varying; not invoice-matched) (Farmland Info guide).
Application practice (NRCS)

Incorporate when possible (tillage, trench, drill, beds, fertigation); surface-only risks wind/water loss (FAQ)
Inoculate with compost, compost tea, or manure (2022 PDF)
Pasture OK; native rangeland only if facilitating CPS 550 or 342 (FAQ)
Lifespan 1 year; up to 5 applications over a contract (FAQ)
Ranking improves when bundled with other soil-health practices (cover crops, no-till, rotations, etc.) (FAQ)

Full methods note: Application Rates and Methods.

Contaminants and Quality
PAH and process quality
Reviews and empirical papers show PAH content depends on feedstock, temperature, vapor residence, and especially post-pyrolysis vapor condensation. Clean process design + batch testing against EBC/IBI limits is the practical consensus.
Heavy metals, high salts (manure chars), dioxins/furans, and PCBs are also quality concerns for soil use—see market-side safeguards in MRV Stack and Risks and Controversies.

Elemental ratios: H/C_org ≤ 0.7; O/C_org often ≤ 0.4 (see Properties)

Production/Feedstocks.title: Feedstocks
Production/Feedstocks.content:
Feedstocks
Brief hub for biomass inputs to biochar. Existing notes already cover how feedstock changes carbon fraction and chemistry; this page tracks what still needs dedicated research rather than inventing inventory data.
What we already know (in vault)

Production — feedstock is a primary control alongside temperature and residence time; woody/low-ash chars often ~50–90% C; manure/sludge and gasification residues are much lower (Woolf et al., 2021 examples in that note).
Properties — ash, nutrients, pH, and CEC vary widely with feedstock class; H/C_org and O/C_org remain the usual persistence proxies.
Contaminants and Quality — sludge, treated wood, and some manures raise contaminant and eligibility questions for product standards and credit methodologies.

Why feedstock choice matters





























DimensionWhy it mattersCarbon yield & permanence proxiesSets how much durable C per tonne feedstockContaminantsPAH / heavy-metal risk; eligibility under EBC/IBI and registriesCompeting usesBiomass may already be fuel, feed, or soil organic matterLogisticsMoisture, density, seasonality, and transport costAdditionality / baselineCredit programs care whether feedstock would have decayed or burned

Production Hub
Map of notes on how biochar is made, what feedstock and process choices control, and how material quality is judged before application or credit issuance. This domain sits between raw biomass and the science of permanence / agronomy / markets.
Domain purpose
Production is the controllable step that turns biomass into a carbon-rich solid. Peak temperature, residence time, heating rate, reactor type, and feedstock chemistry jointly set:

Mass yield of char vs oil/gas
Carbon content and aromatic condensation (persistence proxies such as H/C_org, O/C_org)
Ash, nutrients, pH, porosity, and contaminant risk

Credit programs and product standards (EBC/IBI, CSI, Puro, Verra, Isometric) all depend on production data and lab characterization—see MRV Stack and Contaminants and Quality.

Production
Process
Thermochemical decomposition of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin yields:

Solid — biochar
Liquids — bio-oil
Gases — CO₂, CO, H₂, light hydrocarbons

Typical ranges




















ModeTemperature / rateFavorsSlow pyrolysis~300–700 °C, low heating rate, minutes–hoursBiochar yieldFast / flash pyrolysisHigher heating rates, shorter residenceLiquids
Controls on properties

Feedstock (wood, herbaceous, manure, sludge, shells…)
Peak temperature, residence time, heating rate
Reactor design, ash content

Carbon content
Commonly ~50–90% C by mass for woody/low-ash chars; much lower for high-ash manure/sludge or gasification residues (Woolf et al., 2021).
Carbon fraction examples (Woolf et al., 2021)





























Feedstock / processApprox. FCWood pyrolysis (mean)≈ 0.76High-T wood≈ 0.81Manure pyrolysis≈ 0.39Sewage sludge pyrolysis≈ 0.37Gasification sludge/manure~0.10–0.14
Process effects (summary)
Higher pyrolysis T → lower H/C_org & O/C_org, higher aromatic condensation, generally higher F_perm, often higher pH/surface area, lower volatile matter and sometimes lower yield. Gasification chars can be very high-ash / low FC; permanence may still be high if H/C_org is low, but agronomic C per tonne is lower.

Science/CDR-Potential-and-IPCC-Accountin.title: CDR Potential and IPCC Accounting
Science/CDR-Potential-and-IPCC-Accountin.content:
CDR Potential and IPCC Accounting
IPCC inventory method
IPCC 2019 Refinement Vol. 4 Appendix 4 provides a method for estimating biochar C in mineral cropland/grassland soils (PDF).
F_perm after 100 years (conservative ~20 °C basis in appendix notes):





















Temperature classF_permLow (350–450 °C)0.65Medium (450–600 °C)0.80High (>600 °C / high-T gasification)0.89
Uncertainty roughly ±11–15%. Guidance / basis for future Tier 1—not a credit methodology. See Verra VM0044, Puro CORC200+, etc. for market methods.
Woolf et al. (2021) extends this with H/C_org and soil-temperature predictors. DOI: 10.1021/acs.est.1c02425.
Mitigation / CDR potential estimates





























SourceEstimateWoolf et al. 2010Max 1.8 Pg CO₂-Cₑ yr⁻¹ (≈ ~6.6 Pg CO₂e if ×44/12); century total 130 Pg CO₂-Cₑ. Prefer Lehmann 2021 / Weng 2025 for updated framing.Lehmann et al. 2021Emission reductions 3.4–6.3 Pg CO₂e yr⁻¹ (~half CDR); residues-only 2.4–3.9; with land sparing + CCS up to ~7.4–10.3Weng & Cowie 2025Literature 0.03–11; credible multi-Gt scaleState of CDR 2026 (Fuss et al.)Sustainable removal ≤~2.7 GtCO₂ yr⁻¹; total mitigation ≤~10.3; IAM 2050 <0.1–1.1Costs (Fuss et al. 2026)Often ~70–360/tCO₂** (recent); broader historical **~10–345
LCA / system boundaries
Net climate benefit is dominated by biochar C permanence vs baseline biomass fate, modulated by methane avoidance (rice, landfill), energy co-products, transport, and kiln CH₄ if poorly engineered (Roberts et al. 2010 onward; Matuštík et al. 2020 review; Lehmann 2021).
State of CDR (2026) and Weng & Cowie (2025) place biochar as largest current novel CDR contributor with gigaton-scale technical/sustainable potential but much lower near-term economic/IAM deployment.
MRV accounting insight (science side)
MRV can focus on mass produced × C fraction × permanence factor at the kiln/gate, with application verification—cheaper than full soil flux monitoring (Lehmann 2021). Markets implement this differently—see MRV Stack.

Science/Consensus-vs-Debates.title: Consensus vs Debates
Science/Consensus-vs-Debates.content:
Consensus vs Debates
Broad consensus

Well-made biochar (adequate T / low H/C_org) is much more persistent than raw biomass; fused aromatics are the mechanistic basis.
Sustainable feedstock (wastes/residues; no deforestation) is required for net climate benefit.
Biochar can raise yields especially in acid/degraded/tropical soils, but responses are context-specific.
N₂O reductions are real in many systems in year 1; magnitude and multi-year persistence less certain.
MRV can focus on mass × C fraction × permanence factor at the kiln/gate, with application verification—cheaper than full soil flux monitoring (Lehmann 2021).
Quality control for PAHs/heavy metals and process emissions (kiln CH₄) matters for safe deployment.

Open debates / uncertainties

Long-term decay model form: Two-pool fits from ≤few-year incubations may mis-estimate millennial recalcitrant pools; newer proxies (HyPy, conductivity, Ro) and policy commentaries argue for refined permanence metrics.
CH₄ in paddies: Direction and magnitude still study-dependent.
Priming ceiling: Decade-scale negative priming is promising but long-term saturation and organic-soil risks remain.
Energy vs CDR trade-off: Relative benefit depends on what energy is displaced (coal vs renewables); as grids decarbonize, soil biochar becomes relatively more attractive (Lehmann 2021).
Economic vs technical potential: Technical/sustainable multi-Gt ≠ near-term deployable; IAM/economic potentials often ≪1 Gt by 2050.
Non-soil uses (concrete, asphalt, animal feed, materials): permanence pathways differ; soil-amendment science does not automatically transfer.
Climate feedback on permanence: Warmer soils accelerate decay (Woolf et al. 2021 Q10 framework)—future warming reduces F_perm relative to today’s tables.

Science/Overview-and-Definition.title: Overview and Definition
Science/Overview-and-Definition.content:
Overview and Definition
Definition
Biochar is a solid, porous, carbon-rich material produced by pyrolysis of biomass under oxygen-free or oxygen-limited conditions.
IUPAC (2024) defines it as a solid multi-functional porous carbonaceous product of agricultural biomass pyrolysis in the temperature range 350–1000 °C, with molar H/C_org < 0.7 and O/C_org < 0.4 to ensure abundant fused aromatic structures and distinguish it from inadequately carbonized materials (Bilias et al., 2024; DOI: 10.1515/pac-2021-0106).
IPCC (2019) inventory appendix defines biochar for GHG accounting as solid material from heating biomass >350 °C under controlled/limited oxidant (pyrolysis or gasification), applicable to mineral soils in cropland/grassland (IPCC 2019 Refinement, Vol. 4, Appendix 4).
Not the same as

























MaterialDistinctionCharcoalTraditionally fuel / metallurgyActivated carbonFurther activated for sorptionHydrocharHydrothermal carbonization; typically higher H/C, less aromaticBiocoal / torrefied biomassMainly energy fuel

Science/Permanence.title: Permanence
Science/Permanence.content:
Permanence
Biochar C mineralizes 1–2 orders of magnitude more slowly than unpyrolysed biomass because of fused aromatic structure (Lehmann et al., 2021). Persistence depends on material chemistry (aromatic condensation) and environment (soil temperature, moisture, minerals, microbes). It is probabilistic / centennial–millennial for well-made chars—not literal forever (Schmidt et al., 2025; Woolf et al., 2021).
Policy / accounting proxies

H/C_org (preferred when measured)
Pyrolysis temperature class
Hydropyrolysis-resistant C (BC_HyPy)
Solid electric conductivity
Reflectance (Ro)

(Woolf et al., 2021; Hagemann/Sanei lines of work cited in Schmidt 2025.)
Key quantitative findings

























SourceFindingIPCC 2019 App. 4F_perm (100 yr): 0.65 (350–450 °C), 0.80 (450–600 °C), 0.89 (>600 °C / high-T gasification); ±~11–15%Woolf et al. 2021At 14.9 °C (global cropland mean), 100-yr F_perm ≈ 0.63 / 0.71 / 0.82 (low/med/high T). At 1000 yr much lower (e.g. high-T ~0.25 at 14.9 °C)Lehmann et al. 2021Of biochars with H/C_org < 0.5, 95% showed >50% C remaining after 100 yr (mean ~82% in that subset)Spokas 2010O/C-based half-life classes (approximate rule-of-thumb; not inventory-grade alone)
Practice takeaway: Prefer H/C_org + soil temperature for project accounting; use IPCC T-class when only production data exist; do not claim “permanent” without a time horizon (usually 100 years in policy).
Active frontier
Ongoing debate (2024–2026) on whether two-pool incubations overestimate long-term decay of the recalcitrant pool—treat as active research, not settled. See Consensus vs Debates and Permanence Science for Credits.

Science/Recent-Research-2021-2026.title: Recent Research 2021-2026
Science/Recent-Research-2021-2026.content:
Recent Research 2021–2026
Major reviews & methods (climate / permanence / accounting)


Lehmann et al. (2021). Biochar in climate change mitigation. Nature Geoscience 14:883–892. DOI: 10.1038/s41561-021-00852-8. Global system potential 3.4–6.3 Pg CO₂e yr⁻¹ emission reductions (~half CDR); with land sparing/CCS pathways up to ~7.4–10.3 Pg CO₂e yr⁻¹. Emphasizes H/C_org, feedstock sustainability, energy vs sequestration trade-offs.


Woolf et al. (2021). Greenhouse Gas Inventory Model for Biochar Additions to Soil. Environ. Sci. Technol. 55:14795–14805. DOI: 10.1021/acs.est.1c02425. ~183 citations (S2). Operational EF model extending IPCC 2019; F_perm from T class or H/C_org; temperature-adjusted.


IPCC (2019). 2019 Refinement… Vol. 4 Appendix 4. PDF. F_perm after 100 yr: 0.65 / 0.80 / 0.89 for low / medium / high T.


Bilias et al. (2024). Glossary of terms used in biochar research (IUPAC Technical Report). Pure Appl. Chem. DOI: 10.1515/pac-2021-0106. Formal terminology (178 terms).


Weng & Cowie (2025). Estimates vary but credible evidence points to gigaton-scale… Commun. Earth Environ. DOI: 10.1038/s43247-025-02228-x. Literature range ~0.03–11 Pg CO₂e yr⁻¹; credible centering around multi-Gt scale.


Fuss et al. (2026). Chapter 10: Costs and potentials. In The State of Carbon Dioxide Removal, 3rd ed. DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/FBZ4X. Sustainable removal up to ~2.7 GtCO₂ yr⁻¹; total mitigation up to ~10.3 GtCO₂ yr⁻¹; IAM Highest Ambition <0.1–1.1 GtCO₂ yr⁻¹ by 2050; costs often US$70–360/tCO₂.


Schmidt et al. (2025). Biochar Permanence—A Policy Commentary. GCB Bioenergy. DOI: 10.1111/gcbb.70092. Centuries–millennia for condensed fractions; multi-proxy discussion.


Soil amendments, crop yields, GHG fluxes


Jia et al. (2023). Global patterns… soil GHG fluxes and crop yield. Land Degradation & Development. DOI: 10.1002/ldr.4868. 3883 paired obs / 220 studies: yield +9.4%; CH₄ −13.0%; N₂O −26.8%; GWP −7.7%.


Global field vs lab synthesis (2022). Renewable & Sustainable Energy Reviews. Field: yield +15.7%, CH₄ −14.8%, N₂O −23.1%, SOC stocks +26.6%.


Jeffery et al. (2017). Biochar boosts tropical but not temperate crop yields. Environ. Res. Lett. 12:053001. DOI: 10.1088/1748-9326/aa67bd — still widely cited.


Ye et al. (2020). Biochar effects on crop yields with and without fertilizer… Soil Use Manage. 36:2–18 — used heavily in Lehmann 2021.


Weng et al. (2017). Biochar built soil carbon over a decade… Nature Climate Change 7:371–376. DOI: 10.1038/nclimate3276. ~344 citations — decade-scale negative priming / rhizodeposit stabilization.


Blanco-Canqui et al. (2020). Soil carbon increased by twice the amount of biochar carbon applied after 6 years… GCB Bioenergy 12:240–251.


Contaminants / process
PAH content depends on feedstock, T, vapor residence, and especially post-pyrolysis vapor condensation. Clean process design + batch testing against EBC/IBI limits is the practical consensus. See Contaminants and Quality; product limits: EBC / IBI.

Science/Terra-Preta-and-Pyrogenic-Carbon.title: Terra Preta and Pyrogenic Carbon
Science/Terra-Preta-and-Pyrogenic-Carbon.content:
Terra Preta and Pyrogenic Carbon
Amazonian Dark Earths (Terra Preta) are the cultural and historical inspiration for modern biochar research: anthropogenic soils enriched with pyrogenic carbon that remain fertile centuries after formation.
Foundational citation
Glaser et al. (2001). The ‘Terra Preta’ phenomenon: a model for sustainable agriculture in the humid tropics. Naturwissenschaften 88:37–41. DOI: 10.1007/s001140000193. ~1,145 citations (Semantic Scholar, 2026-09-14).
This historical analog underpins the idea that intentionally produced pyrogenic carbon can improve tropical soils and store carbon for long periods—later formalized in Lehmann (2006/2007) and modern CDR literature (see Foundational Papers).
